--- title: "{{< fa brands python >}} Python Quick Guide" jupyter: python3 --- Most of you know some R. Here is the translation, covering enough to get through the first month. ::: {#44d93ca6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd DATA = "https://lucymcgowan.github.io/sta-363-f26/data/" Auto = pd.read_csv(DATA + "Auto.csv") ``` ::: ## R to Python | Task | R | Python | |---|---|---| | read a csv | `read_csv("f.csv")` | `pd.read_csv("f.csv")` | | first rows | `head(d)` | `d.head()` | | dimensions | `dim(d)` | `d.shape` | | column names | `names(d)` | `d.columns` | | one column | `d$mpg` | `d["mpg"]` | | several columns | `d[, c("mpg", "weight")]` | `d[["mpg", "weight"]]` | | filter rows | `d[d$mpg > 30, ]` | `d[d["mpg"] > 30]` | | new column | `d$kpl <- d$mpg * 0.425` | `d["kpl"] = d["mpg"] * 0.425` | | summary | `summary(d)` | `d.describe()` | | counts | `table(d$origin)` | `d["origin"].value_counts()` | | mean | `mean(d$mpg)` | `d["mpg"].mean()` | | group means | `aggregate(mpg ~ origin, d, mean)` | `d.groupby("origin")["mpg"].mean()` | | sequence | `1:10` | `range(1, 11)` | | length | `length(x)` | `len(x)` | | missing | `is.na(x)` | `x.isna()` | Two differences that trip people up. Python counts from **zero**, so `d.iloc[0]` is the first row. And `range(1, 11)` **excludes** the endpoint, so it stops at 10. ## Selecting ::: {#769e16d8 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} Auto[["mpg", "horsepower", "weight"]].head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
mpg horsepower weight
0 18.0 130 3504
1 15.0 165 3693
2 18.0 150 3436
``` ::: ::: ::: {#72bf6f05 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} Auto[Auto["mpg"] > 40][["name", "mpg"]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
name mpg
242 volkswagen rabbit custom diesel 43.1
307 vw rabbit 41.5
320 mazda glc 46.6
322 datsun 210 40.8
323 vw rabbit c (diesel) 44.3
324 vw dasher (diesel) 43.4
327 honda civic 1500 gl 44.6
388 vw pickup 44.0
``` ::: ::: Two conditions need `&` for and, `|` for or, and parentheses around each piece: ::: {#0ed614fe .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} Auto[(Auto["mpg"] > 30) & (Auto["year"] > 78)].shape ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` (60, 9) ``` ::: ::: ## The four lines that fit every model Every method this semester, from linear regression to a neural network, uses the same four steps. Learn them once. ::: {#debcf71a .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression X = Auto[["horsepower", "weight"]] # predictors, always a data frame y = Auto["mpg"] # response, always a single column model = LinearRegression() # 1. choose model.fit(X, y) # 2. fit model.predict(X.head(3)) # 3. predict ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` array([19.18811123, 16.43741528, 18.63605667]) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#764fe560 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} model.score(X, y) # 4. score ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` 0.7063752737298348 ``` ::: ::: Swap `LinearRegression()` for `KNeighborsRegressor(5)` or `RandomForestRegressor()` and the other three lines stay as they are. That consistency is why we use scikit-learn. ## Pipelines A pipeline glues preprocessing to the model so they always travel together. This matters more than it looks like it does, and we spend a whole class on why. ::: {#be166568 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsRegressor(10)) pipe.fit(X, y) pipe.score(X, y) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` 0.7794013249655986 ``` ::: ::: ## Plotting ::: {#bfe2fcda .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5)) ax.scatter(Auto["horsepower"], Auto["mpg"], s=12, alpha=0.6, color="#d5008f") ax.set_xlabel("horsepower") ax.set_ylabel("mpg") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](python-guide_files/figure-html/cell-9-output-1.png){} ::: ::: The pattern is always the same: make a `fig` and an `ax`, draw on the `ax`, label the axes, then `plt.show()`. ## Errors you will see **`NameError: name 'X' is not defined`** You did not run the cell that created `X`, or the runtime restarted. Run your cells from the top. **`KeyError: 'mpg'`** That column does not exist. Check `Auto.columns` for the exact spelling. Column names are case sensitive. **`ValueError: Expected 2D array, got 1D array instead`** scikit-learn wants predictors as a data frame. Use `Auto[["horsepower"]]` with two sets of brackets, not `Auto["horsepower"]`. **`SettingWithCopyWarning`** You modified a slice of a data frame. Add `.copy()` when you subset something you intend to change. More in [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.qmd). ## What you will not be graded on You are not being assessed on whether you can recall syntax. Look things up. Use the documentation, use these pages, use an assistant if it helps you understand what the code does. You are being assessed on whether you can reason about models: which one to use, how to tell whether it is any good, and what the output means.
